name: Driftwatch
one_liner: For the platform/AI-engineering team that owns production agents, Driftwatch watches the vendor surfaces those agents depend on — MCP tool schemas, model IDs, API docs and changelogs — and turns each change into a ranked "this will break these 3 agent flows, here's the diff and the fix PR" alert instead of a wall of release notes.
problem: Teams now ship agents that call dozens of third-party tools: MCP servers, provider APIs (Stripe, Slack, Jira, Salesforce), aggregator gateways, and model endpoints. Those surfaces change weekly and silently: a tool's JSON schema gains a required field, an enum value is renamed, a model ID is deprecated, rate-limit or pricing terms change, a gateway reshapes its response. The agent doesn't throw a clean 500 — it degrades: the LLM mis-fills an argument, retries, loops, burns tokens, or returns a confidently wrong answer. Today the owning engineer finds out from a customer complaint or a spike in a Langfuse/Datadog trace dashboard, then spends hours bisecting whether the regression came from their prompt, their model, or the vendor. The "stay informed" workaround is exactly what @mattyp built by hand in the first bookmark: a bespoke bot that polls one vendor's changelog page and DMs the release notes. That approach scales to one vendor and one reader, it has no notion of which changes matter to *your* code, and generic change-detection tools (Visualping, PageCrawl) deliver "this page changed" diffs with no mapping to the agent flows that break.
target_customer: Paying buyer: the engineering manager or staff engineer who owns agents in production at a 20–500 person software company (AI-native SaaS, fintech ops automation, support automation). Persona: "the person on call when the agent stops booking meetings." Secondary buyer later: platform/AppSec teams already standing up MCP gateways and approved-tool registries, who need change control on those registries. Budget sits in the existing dev-tooling line next to Sentry/Datadog/Langfuse; estimate $300–$1,500/month per team at seed/Series A size.
why_now: Three things changed in the last ~12 months. (1) Agents in production now depend on large external tool surfaces — Monid alone advertises 1,700+ tools across 55+ providers and shows hundreds of thousands of weekly calls routed to single providers, so the dependency count per agent has exploded. (2) MCP is now the common wire format, which means tool schemas are machine-readable and diffable — you can compute "required field added" automatically, which was impossible when every integration was bespoke SDK code. (3) Model and API deprecation cadence from the big labs is fast and consequential, and enterprises are already building allowlists and private MCP registries (Tyk, WSO2, TrueFoundry, Microsoft Foundry guidance) — registries create the hook where change-control naturally lives.
comparables: Visualping (visualping.io) and PageCrawl (pagecrawl.io) — general website/changelog change detection with AI summaries and Slack alerts; PageCrawl even publishes posts on monitoring AI-vendor deprecation pages. Gap: they diff pages, not schemas, and have zero knowledge of your codebase, so they cannot say which of your agent flows breaks. LaunchNotes (launchnotes.com, enterprise tier reported from ~$249/mo for two users per a competitor comparison page) and AnnounceKit — outbound release-note publishing for vendors, the opposite direction of our product. Langfuse, LangSmith, Braintrust, Laminar, Datadog LLM Observability — agent tracing, evals and per-tool cost analytics; they show you the regression after it happens in your traces, but they don't watch the vendor side or attribute a failure to a specific upstream schema change. MCP gateways (Tyk, TrueFoundry, Zuplo, WSO2) — allowlists, auth and policy for which servers agents may call; they govern access, not version drift and blast radius. Monid (monid.ai) — one-integration access to 1,800+ tools plus a usage leaderboard; it is a distribution surface and a potential partner/data source, not a change-impact product. Honest uncertainty: I did not find a funded company doing vendor-schema-diff → your-agent blast radius specifically; my searches for that exact wedge returned nothing, which could mean the gap is real or that the category is named something I did not search.
market_note: Estimate, stated as such. Assume ~20k–40k companies worldwide will run agents with external tool calls in production by 2027 (rough extrapolation from current LLM-observability customer bases, not a measured figure). At a $500/mo average and 5% reachable penetration in three years that is roughly $60M ARR of addressable spend — a real but not enormous standalone market, which argues for this being either a fast-moving independent tool or an eventual module inside an observability or MCP-gateway platform. Willingness to pay is anchored by what teams already pay for Sentry and LLM observability; the pitch is "one prevented silent agent outage pays for the year," which is a credible but unproven claim until a design partner confirms incident frequency and cost.
risks: 1) Blast-radius mapping may be too shallow to trust. Connecting "Stripe MCP added a required `idempotency_scope` field" to "your refund-handling agent will break" requires reading the customer's agent code or trace history accurately; if the mapping is wrong half the time, it becomes another noisy alert channel and gets muted. 2) It may be a feature, not a company. Langfuse/Braintrust/Datadog already hold the traces and could add "upstream change correlated with this regression" in a quarter; MCP gateways already sit in the call path and could version-pin and diff schemas natively. 3) Coverage cost. Keeping up with hundreds of vendor changelogs, docs sites and MCP registries is ongoing scraping/normalisation grind with no moat unless you capture proprietary data (e.g. observed schema changes across customers before they're announced).
riskiest_assumptions: 1) Silent tool-contract drift is a real, recurring and expensive incident class — not an occasional annoyance. Must be true first: if teams say "it happens twice a year and we fix it in an hour," there is no budget. 2) A useful blast-radius verdict can be produced from cheap inputs (the agent's tool manifest plus a sample of traces) without deep static analysis of the customer's whole codebase. 3) The buyer will connect something — a repo, a gateway, or trace export — within one call. If the only honest answer requires a security review, the sales cycle kills the wedge.
first_customers: Ten specific, findable targets: (a) teams visible in the Monid rankings and its provider list — the companies whose tools are being called hundreds of thousands of times a week, plus their heaviest consumers; (b) engineers posting in the Langfuse, LangChain and MCP GitHub discussions about tool-schema breakage (the GitHub community thread on org-level MCP allowlists is a live list of named enterprise engineers); (c) YC W25/S25/W26 companies whose product description includes "agent" and who publicly list integrations — ~30 of them, reachable by founder-to-founder cold email; (d) attendees/speakers at MCP and AI-engineering meetups in SF and NYC. Opening line is a free one-off report: "here are the 7 changes in your 12 declared tools over the last 60 days and the 2 that probably affected you."
validation_test: This week: pick 12 widely used MCP servers / tool APIs, snapshot their tool schemas and changelogs daily for 7 days, and hand-build the diff report. Then cold-email 25 engineers who own production agents (sourced from the lists above) with a personalised version: "your stack uses 4 of these; 2 changed in a way that alters required arguments — want the report?" Pass signal: 5+ replies, and 3+ who say on a call that they have been burned by this at least once in the last quarter AND agree to connect a repo or trace export to a design-partner pilot. Fail signal: people find the report interesting but cannot name a single incident it would have prevented — that means it's a newsletter, not a product.
reasoning: Four candidates were credible; this one won on buyer clarity and wedge narrowness. The @mattyp bookmark is the tell: a sophisticated builder hand-rolled a bot whose entire job is "watch one vendor's changelog and tell me what changed." That is a personal workaround for a problem that becomes expensive, not merely annoying, the moment the consumer of the change is an autonomous agent rather than a human reader. The Monid bookmark supplies the scale argument — agents now reach across 1,700+ tools from 55+ providers, so per-team dependency counts have jumped an order of magnitude — and the poteto bookmark supplies the cultural proof that engineers are now willing to spend real effort proving their agent-written systems behave correctly. Research showed the two adjacent categories are genuinely adjacent, not overlapping: change-detection tools (Visualping, PageCrawl) diff pages with no model of your code, and agent-observability tools (Langfuse, Braintrust, Datadog) diff your traces with no model of the vendor. Nobody I found closes the loop between them. The failure mode I most believe — "this is a feature Langfuse ships next quarter" — is also the most survivable one for a narrow first version, because the wedge (a weekly one-page impact report derived from a tool manifest) can be sold before anyone integrates anything, and can be acquired or repositioned as a gateway add-on if the incumbents move.
candidates_considered:
1) Driftwatch — vendor change → agent blast radius. WON: clear technical buyer, measurable pain, visible whitespace between change-detection and observability.
2) "Agent tool spend control plane" — per-tool budgets, caps and ROI reporting on top of gateways like Monid. LOST: Langfuse, Braintrust, Datadog and the gateways themselves already ship per-tool cost analytics; the buyer and workflow are identical to incumbents, so the gap is closed.
3) Formal-verification-as-a-service for agent-written code (from @poteto's pstack / TLA+ skill). LOST on wedge and market pull: the people who can write a correct TLA+ model are the people who don't need to buy it, the ones who need it can't judge whether the model is right, and the hard part is spec-authoring judgement, not tooling. Research showed academic and incumbent activity (Azure storage specs, Datadog harness work) but no normal-team buyer with budget.
4) Structured real-time data for vertical agents (from the Tako/Vercel bookmark) — e.g. sourced structured feeds for a specific vertical. LOST: Tako is funded ($5.75M seed, Oct 2024) and already distributing via Vercel AI Gateway at $7–12 per 1,000 requests; proposing a near-identical data API would be a thin clone.
5) "AI board of advisors" / second-brain productivity skills (nateherk, tsukiema_ bookmarks). LOST: prompt packs, not products — no defensibility, no clear B2B buyer, and trivially replicated inside the assistants themselves.
Skipped as noise or non-actionable: @jack/Dessa (a Block research preview, not a gap), @dwarkesh_sp transistor video, @davidsenra/dhh commentary, @ryangrowthh link-only post with no title or description.
research_notes: Used 11 of 12 tool calls. Two Web Summary calls resolved the thin bookmarks: Monid (confirmed it is a runtime tool gateway + usage leaderboard, 1,700+ tools / 55+ providers, rankings current to 2026-10-20 with TinyFish at 754K weekly calls — this is what convinced me the tool-dependency surface is now large enough to need change control) and Tako/Vercel (confirmed $5.75M seed and live Gateway pricing of $7–12 per 1,000 requests, which killed candidate 4 as a clone). A third summary explained pstack's /create-formal-verification-skill in enough detail to see that its value is judgement-dependent, which demoted candidate 3. Searches then tested each surviving candidate: agent cost observability returned Langfuse, Braintrust, Laminar, Datadog, LangSmith all doing per-tool-call cost breakdowns, closing that gap; changelog/change monitoring returned Visualping, PageCrawl, LaunchNotes, AnnounceKit — all either page-diffing or outbound publishing, neither mapping to code; MCP governance searches returned Tyk, WSO2, TrueFoundry, Zuplo and Microsoft Foundry doing allowlists and registries but not version-drift impact. Two targeted searches for the exact wedge (agent contract testing / schema-drift alerting as a product) returned essentially nothing, which is why the brief flags that absence as weak evidence rather than proof of whitespace. I could not view any images or videos in the bookmarks and did not speculate about their contents. Scoring: Pain 8, Market pull 7, Timing 9, Gap 7, Wedge 7 → 7.6.
prototype_summary: Driftwatch turns 14 noisy vendor changelog/schema entries into a ranked impact board showing exactly which of your 6 AI agent flows break, where, and the one-line fix.
